words.meaning: the state of becoming outdated and no longer useful
words.example: Engineers now design phone batteries with planned obsolescence in mind, knowing users will replace the device within three years.

words.meaning: the removal of middlemen between producers and consumers, made possible by technology
words.example: Streaming platforms completed the disintermediation of the music industry, letting artists reach listeners without record labels.

words.meaning: allowing everything to be seen or watched at once
words.example: Smart cities are becoming panoptic environments where cameras track every pedestrian's movement.

words.meaning: a design detail that copies the look of a real-world object into a digital product
words.example: The leather texture on that old calendar app was a skeuomorph meant to comfort paper-and-pen users.

words.meaning: a complex system whose inner workings are hidden from its users
words.example: Large language models are often black boxes: even their creators cannot fully explain every answer they produce.

words.meaning: a confident but completely false output generated by an AI
words.example: That chatbot's hallucination about a nonexistent law briefly fooled a busy lawyer.
words.persian: توهم مصنوعی (پاسخ نادرست مطمئنانهٔ هوش مصنوعی)

words.meaning: a fake video or audio clip made with artificial intelligence
words.example: The viral video of the mayor confessing to bribery turned out to be a crude deepfake.

words.meaning: the hypothetical moment when artificial intelligence surpasses human intelligence
words.example: Some futurists predict the singularity will arrive within our lifetime; others call it science fiction.

words.meaning: a person who opposes or distrusts new technology
words.example: The neoluddite in our office refuses to use the cloud and still backs up everything on printed paper.

words.meaning: the process of turning every aspect of life into data that can be collected and analyzed
words.example: Fitness trackers are a symbol of datafication: even sleep has become a set of numbers.

grammar.title: Ability and possibility at C2: can, could, could have, be able to
grammar.explanation:
**CAN** is present or future ability, simple and direct: I **can** spot a deepfake after one viewing. It also covers general possibility: technology **can** surprise us all.

**COULD** is the past of **can** for general ability: early phones **could** barely hold a charge. It also softens a present or future possibility: the singularity **could** arrive quietly, through updates.

For everything **can** and **could** cannot do — perfect forms, infinitives, gerunds — use **BE ABLE TO**. I'd love to **be able to** explain that black box. She has **been able to** resist datafication so far.

**COULD HAVE** + past participle looks backward at a dead possibility. We **could have** slowed obsolescence if the law had required longer support. It judges a chance that was never taken.

**CAN'T** is present impossibility: you **can't** unsee a panoptic city. **COULDN'T** is past: early apps **couldn't** process video. The formal past negative is **WASN'T ABLE TO**.

Formal writing prefers **be able to** over **can**. The committee **was able to** confirm the hallucination within an hour sounds measured and academic; **could** would sound conversational in the same report.
examples: I *can* spot a deepfake after one viewing. (present ability)
Early phones *could* barely hold a charge. (past general ability)
The singularity *could* arrive quietly, through updates. (softened future possibility)
I'd love to *be able to* explain that black box. (infinitive: no form of can exists)
She has *been able to* resist datafication so far. (perfect form)
We *could have* slowed obsolescence if the law had required longer support. (unrealized past possibility)
You *can't* unsee a panoptic city. (present impossibility)
Early apps *couldn't* process video in real time. (past inability)
The committee *was able to* confirm the hallucination within an hour. (formal register)

practice.q: Can 'could' describe a single completed action in the past, like 'I could repair the server yesterday'?
practice.a: No — for a single completed past action use 'was able to': 'I was able to repair the server yesterday.' 'Could' works only for general past ability: 'I could repair any server back then.'

practice.q: Why is 'I will can detect deepfakes' wrong?
practice.a: 'Can' has no future form. Use 'be able to': 'I will be able to detect deepfakes.' The same fix works after infinitives and perfects: 'to be able to', 'have been able to'.

practice.q: What is the difference between 'We could stop the disintermediation' and 'We could have stopped the disintermediation'?
practice.a: 'Could stop' is still possible — the door is open. 'Could have stopped' means the chance is gone; the disintermediation already happened and we missed our moment.
